title: Madhavan Folds His Hands, Mammootty Walks Tall, and an Empty Chair for Satish Shah: Cinema's Padma Roll Call
excerpt: President Murmu honours R. Madhavan, Mammootty and Alka Yagnik at the second Padma Awards 2026 ceremony — while a posthumous Padma Shri for Satish Shah hits the diaspora hardest.
body:
The Durbar Hall at Rashtrapati Bhavan does a strange thing to film stars. Strip away the arc lights, the fan chants, the carefully art-directed entrances, and what's left is a man in a bandhgala walking toward President **Droupadi Murmu** with his hands folded, suddenly looking less like a hero and more like everyone's favourite uncle who finally got his due. On Tuesday, that man was **R. Madhavan** — and by the time he'd posted his note, the whole diaspora was a little misty.

This was the second investiture ceremony of Padma Awards 2026, and the President conferred honours on 65 distinguished personalities across cinema, sport, science and public service. The film fraternity, as ever, brought the cameras. Malayalam superstar **Mammootty** received the Padma Bhushan — the higher honour — and walked in with the kind of quiet command no spotlight can manufacture, flanked by his family including son and fellow actor **Dulquer Salmaan**, who has spent the last few years building his own crossover stardom. Playback legend **Alka Yagnik**, the voice behind three decades of Hindi cinema's most-streamed love songs, was honoured with the Padma Bhushan too; battling health issues, she was assisted to the dais, and was later seen seeking blessings from Prime Minister **Narendra Modi** in a moment that needed no soundtrack.

And then there was the absence that landed hardest.

> "To every person who watched my films, embraced my characters, celebrated my successes, forgave my shortcomings, and stood by me through the years — this honor belongs as much to you as it does to me." — R. Madhavan

Madhavan, 56, was recommended for the Padma Shri by the Government of Maharashtra, and his acceptance note read like a man genuinely undone by it. There's a particular sweetness to this one. This is the actor who made an entire generation fall for **Maddy** in *Alaipayuthey* and *Rehnaa Hai Terre Dil Mein*, who reinvented himself as the heart of *3 Idiots*, then directed and starred in *Rocketry* as a one-man crusade. He has crossed Tamil, Hindi and Telugu industries with a rare ease — which is exactly why, for NRIs who grew up watching him in three languages at once, this feels less like a state honour and more like a family milestone. He dedicated it "to the magical world of cinema," and you believed him.


Not every name on the list got to walk to the dais. **Satish Shah** — Sahil from *Sarabhai vs Sarabhai*, the comic timing behind a hundred dinner-table impressions across diaspora living rooms — was awarded the Padma Shri posthumously, his honour accepted by his cousin on his behalf. For a community that streamed *Sarabhai* on loop to keep homesickness at bay, watching that empty space at the ceremony was its own quiet gut-punch. Telugu veteran **Gadde Babu Rajendra Prasad** was also among the cinema honourees, rounding out a list that, for once, stretched genuinely pan-Indian.

The numbers tell their own story of scale. This year, 131 Padma Awards were announced in total — five Padma Vibhushan, 13 Padma Bhushan and 113 Padma Shri — with Tuesday's ceremony honouring 65 recipients, following the first investiture on May 25. Cricketer **Rohit Sharma** picked up his honour the same afternoon, a reminder that in India the line between film stardom and sporting godhood was always more of a suggestion than a rule.

What makes a moment like this travel so well to Edison and Southall and Brampton isn't the medal itself. It's the recognition that the films and songs that raised a generation abroad — the ones playing on a laptop at 2 a.m. when the snow won't stop and home feels impossibly far — were finally being stamped as national treasure by the country that made them. Madhavan put it best when he spoke of "a greater duty," but the real duty was always the diaspora's, quietly keeping these stars alive on repeat across time zones.

You can stream most of the honourees' defining work right now wherever you are: Madhavan's *3 Idiots* and *Rocketry* and Mammootty's vast catalogue sit across Prime Video, Netflix and JioHotstar in the US, UK and Canada, often with subtitles, and *Sarabhai vs Sarabhai* remains a comfort-watch a click away. The medals were pinned on in Delhi. But the applause, as it always has, came from everywhere.
